newsitem.title: USA: Wheat harvest expands in Kansas, yields seen high.
newsitem.headline: Wheat harvest expands in Kansas, yields seen high.

text.p: Hot, dry weather allowed harvesting of the Kansas hard red winter wheat crop to advance rapidly this weekend, and grain merchandisers said Sunday that yields were coming in above average.
Dealers said the crop appeared to have shrugged off the damaging effects of a late-season freeze thanks to cool wet weather during late April and May.
"It's not the crop we would have had before the freeze, but it's still going to be a very good crop from what we've seen so far," a grain dealer in south central Kansas said.
Dealers said that as of Sunday, average yields in southern Kansas were coming in at around 45 bushels per acre (bpa).

"There's one case we heard 70 bushels per acre, but that's an anomaly. I'd say overall we're seeing a lot of mid- to upper-40s. There's quite a few 60s out there, too," the south central Kansas dealer said.

Some dealers speculated that Kansas -- typically the largest producer of HRW wheat -- may produce more than 400 million bushels this year. In its June 12 crop report, USDA estimated 1997 Kansas HRW wheat output at 363.8 million bushels, with an average yield of 34.0 bushels per acre.
In 1996, drought conditions crippled Kansas production, and the state harvested only 255.2 million bushels for an average yield of 29.0 bpa.
Meanwhile, as harvesting continued in Oklahoma, dealers said they were having trouble locating enough trucks to help transport harvested wheat from grain elevators to larger terminals.
Dealers said the problem had become serious enough that wheat was being piled on the ground outside country elevators because of a lack of storage space.
"One elevator manager in Pond Creek (Okla.) said he had 30,000 bushels of wheat on the ground... and that was at 8:51 this morning," a grain merchandiser in north central Okalhoma said.

Dealers said truck shortages were common around harvest time, but that the situation was more serious this year because many people in the grain trade had expected a harvest that was average or below average.
"It's certainly more than they ever dreamed of. Another merchandiser I know feels like Oklahoma will (produce more than) 150 million bushels," the north central Oklahoma merchandiser said.
In its June report, USDA estimated 1997 Oklahoma wheat production at 135.0 million bushels.
"As far as yields go, you can hear anywhere from 10 (bpa) on a bad field to an average of about 48 in the north central part of the state," the Oklahoma dealer said.
